parts.title: My life as a school reporter
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last year, I became the editor of our school newspaper. I was only fourteen, and I did not know much about journalism, but I loved writing and I wanted to learn.

Our team has ten members, and we meet every Wednesday to decide the stories for the next issue. Some people write about sport, others about music or school trips. My favourite job is the interview. Last month, I talked to our head teacher about the new rules for mobile phones, and I was very nervous. She answered all my questions, and she even laughed at one of my jokes.

The hardest part of the work is the deadline. Every article must be ready by Friday at noon, and sometimes, we have to stay late to finish. Once, a page was empty on Thursday night, and we wrote a story about the school cat in just twenty minutes!

The best moment came when a local newspaper printed one of our stories about the town library. I felt so proud. Now I think I would like to become a real journalist, but my mother says that I should become a doctor first.

questions.prompt: How did the writer become the editor?
options: She was keen to learn about it
She knew a lot about journalism
She was chosen by the head teacher
questions.explanation: She did not know much but she loved writing and wanted to learn.

options: They choose stories for the next issue
questions.explanation: They meet to decide the stories for the next issue.

options: She refused to answer some questions

questions.explanation: She answered all the questions and laughed at a joke.

questions.prompt: What is the hardest part of the work?
options: The deadline on Friday at noon
questions.explanation: Every article must be ready by Friday at noon.

questions.prompt: What happened when the local paper printed a story?
options: She won a prize at school
She was asked to join them
She felt proud of the team
questions.explanation: She says she felt so proud.

parts.title: The history of the newspaper
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
The first printed newspapers appeared in Europe about four hundred years ago. [1] They were small, with only a few pages, and they were published once a week.

At that time, most people could not read. [2] Someone would read the news aloud in a café or a market, and everybody gathered around to listen.

In the nineteenth century, new machines made printing much faster. [3] A newspaper could now be sold for a penny, so even poor families could buy one.

The invention of the telegraph helped too. [4] News from other countries could arrive in a few hours instead of several weeks.

Today, many people read the news on their phones. [5] Some newspapers have even stopped printing on paper altogether.
sentences: As a result, the number of readers grew very quickly.
This has changed the business of journalism enormously.
Because of this, reading aloud was an important way to share information.
This was one of the first real breakthroughs in the speed of information.
Nobody had ever seen anything like them before.
The best reporters were paid large sums of money by the kings.

gaps.explanation: Nobody had seen anything like them before leads to the description of them being small.
Because people could not read, reading aloud was important, and the next sentence shows someone reading in a café.
Faster printing led to a quicker growth in readers, and it explains why the price could be a penny.
The speed of information links to news arriving in a few hours.
The change to phones has changed journalism, and some papers stopped printing on paper.

parts.title: How to spot fake news
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: These days, we see news all the time, [1] not everything that we read is true. Some websites write stories that are completely false, [2] they want people to click on them and spend time on their pages. Before you share a story with your friends, you [3] to ask a few questions. Who wrote it? Is the same story on other websites? Does the photo look real? If a story seems too amazing to be true, it is often [4] true. You should also be careful with stories [5] make you very angry or afraid. A good rule is to wait before sharing. If in doubt, check with a teacher or look at [6] trusted website.

gaps.explanation: We see news all the time, but not everything is true: contrast.
They write false stories because they want people to click.
You should ask a few questions before you share: advice.
A story that seems too amazing is often not true.
Stories that make you angry: a relative pronoun for things.
Look at a trusted website: indefinite article before an adjective.

parts.title: A talk about a radio station
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: mariam
turns.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to our radio station. My name is Dinah, and I am the manager. We went on the air twenty years ago, and today we have more than two hundred thousand listeners. Our busiest time is the morning, between seven and nine, when people are driving to work. During this time, we play music, read the news and give traffic reports. In the afternoon, we have a show for children, and on Sundays, we invite local bands to play live in our studio. We have twelve presenters and about thirty volunteers, many of whom are students. If you would like to take part, you can write to us, or you can come on Saturday, when we have an open day. On that day, you can see the studio and talk to our presenters. The best thing about working in radio is that every day is different, so you are never bored.

gaps.explanation: We went on the air twenty years ago.

gaps.explanation: More than two hundred thousand listeners.

gaps.prompt: The busiest time is in the ___
gaps.explanation: Our busiest time is the morning.
On Sundays, we invite local bands to play live.
Come on Saturday, when we have an open day.

parts.title: An interview with a news photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Dorrit, you take pictures for a national newspaper. How did you start?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: I took pictures for my school magazine when I was fifteen. A local paper bought one of them, and I earned twenty pounds. I felt like a millionaire!

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What kinds of events do you cover?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Everything: sports matches, protests, concerts, even floods. I never know in the morning where I will be at night.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the most difficult part of your job?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Waiting. Sometimes, I stand for five hours in the cold to get one good picture. And I must be fast, because the moment is gone in a second.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Have you ever been in danger?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Once, at a big storm, a tree fell very close to me. After that, I always checked the weather and told my editor where I was going.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Which of your pictures are you proudest of?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: A photo of a boy who is hugging his dog after a flood. The dog was missing for three days. Thousands of people wrote to say that it made them cry.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young photographer?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Always carry your camera, and look at the light. And be kind to the people you photograph, because they are not just a subject.
